attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

#!/bin/bash

if [ "$a" -lt -5 ]; then key=-1; else key=$a; fi
if [ "$key" -lt 0 ]; then key=-1; fi

findings.claim: With no argv[1] at all, n defaults to 18. With argv[1] present but the EMPTY STRING, n = 0 (a distinct, observable case) because the C++ guard is `argc > 1`, not "argv[1] is non-empty".
findings.evidence:
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable | head -1  ->  18
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "" | head -1  ->  0
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable | md5sum  ->  a0d2c78ca285231f314d62a97cfe38db
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 18 | md5sum  ->  a0d2c78ca285231f314d62a97cfe38db   (no-arg == n=18 byte-for-byte)

findings.claim: Only argv[1] is consumed; all further argv entries are ignored entirely (they are NOT joined or summed).
findings.evidence:
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 4 99 | md5sum -> fd9376c664ef22b2708b70a5a1128c66

findings.claim: The whitespace skipped before the sign is EXACTLY the six C-locale isspace bytes {0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE}. No other byte in 1..255 is skipped (in particular not 0x85 NEL nor 0xA0, and not UTF-8 NBSP 0xC2 0xA0).
findings.evidence:
Generated all 255 strings chr(b)+"7" (b=1..255) NUL-separated, fed through glibc atoi:
$ /tmp/w/gen2 > /tmp/w/bytes.bin
$ xargs -0 -a /tmp/w/bytes.bin -n 100 /tmp/w/probe | cut -f1 > /tmp/w/c_b.txt
$ head -255 /tmp/w/c_b.txt | grep -n '^7$' | awk -F: '{printf "0x%02x ", $1}'
0x09 0x0a 0x0b 0x0c 0x0d 0x20 0x2b 0x30
(0x2b is '+' giving +7 and 0x30 is '0' giving 07=7 -- neither is whitespace; the whitespace set is the six remaining.)
Direct binary confirmation of one non-space high byte:
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable $'\xc2\xa07'  ->  the n<=0 output (atoi=0), NOT 7

findings.claim: All of \r \n \t \v \f and space are skipped by the real binary, including in combination, and a sign may follow them.
findings.evidence:
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable $'
	\v  7' | md5sum matches the n=7 fingerprint
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable $'

Each of $'	7' $'
7' $'\v7' $' 7' $'7' '   7' independently produced the n=7 output.

findings.claim: Exactly ONE optional sign is accepted, immediately after the whitespace run. A second sign, or a sign after whitespace-after-sign, aborts the parse and yields 0.
findings.evidence:
atoi results (C) and reference-binary output class agree for all of these:
'+5'->5 (n=5 output), '-5'->-5 (n<=0 output), '+0'->0, '-0'->0,
'--5'->0, '++5'->0, '+-3'->0, '-+3'->0, '+ 5'->0, ' +  5'->0, '-'->0, '+'->0, ' -   18'->0
All verified: e.g. $ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable '+ 5' | md5sum == the n<=0 hash a153b11b8ec7c4b38780f930319ae45d

findings.claim: Parsing is base 10 only and stops at the first non-digit; trailing junk is silently ignored (no error, no stderr). Leading zeros are fine and do not trigger octal. '0x'/'0X' prefixes parse as 0.
Values above INT_MAX are TRUNCATED to 32 bits (wrapping), NOT saturated at INT_MAX. This is directly observable: '4294967314' (= 2^32 + 18) makes the program behave exactly as n=18.
findings.evidence:
$ /tmp/w/probe 4294967314   ->  atoi=18   strtol=4294967314
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 4294967314 | md5sum  == the n=18 fingerprint
More wrap families, all confirmed against the binary (55/55 exact fingerprint matches, 0 failures):
'8589934592+k' (2*2^32+k), '7*2^32+k', and negatives '-(2^32-k)' / '-(2*2^32-k)' for k in {0,1,2,3,5,7,11,18,25,100,399}

$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 30064771090 | md5sum == n=18 fingerprint

findings.claim: Negative overflow of int also wraps, not clamps: '-2147483649' yields n = INT_MAX = 2147483647 (a huge positive workload), NOT INT_MIN and NOT 0.
findings.evidence:
$ /tmp/w/probe -2147483649  ->  atoi=2147483647  strtol=-2147483649
$ timeout 4 /workspace/dataset/test18_executable -2147483649 | head -c 60   ->  produced NO output within 4s
$ timeout 4 /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 2147483647  | head -c 60   ->  produced NO output within 4s  (identical behavior)
Contrast: $ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 1000000 prints instantly (first line '1000000'), so 'no output in 4s' is a genuine signal of a ~2^31 workload, not a crash. If the parse had clamped to 0/INT_MIN the n<=0 output would have appeared in microseconds.

findings.claim: Accumulation saturates at the C `long` (i64) boundary FIRST, and only then is truncated to int. So '18446744073709551634' (= 2^64 + 18) gives -1, NOT 18 -- proving the intermediate width is 64-bit signed with saturation, not 64-bit wrapping and not 128-bit.
findings.evidence:
$ /tmp/w/probe 18446744073709551634  ->  atoi=-1  strtol=9223372036854775807
$ /workspace/dataset/test18_executable 18446744073709551634 | md5sum == a153b11b8ec7c4b38780f930319ae45d (the n<=0 output)
If it had wrapped mod 2^64 the answer would be 18 and the n=18 output would have appeared. It did not.
Same for '-18446744073709551598' (= -(2^64 - 18)): $ /tmp/w/probe -> atoi=0, strtol=-9223372036854775808; binary gives the n<=0 output, not n=18.

findings.claim: Positive overflow of long saturates to LONG_MAX (0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF) whose low 32 bits are 0xFFFFFFFF, so every over-LONG_MAX positive string yields n = -1. Negative overflow saturates to LONG_MIN (0x8000_0000_0000_0000) whose low 32 bits are 0, so every over-LONG_MIN negative string yields n = 0. Both land in the n<=0 output class.

'-9223372036854775808' (exactly LONG_MIN) yields 0, and a Rust parser that accumulates the magnitude in i64 and flags overflow at 9223372036854775808 still produces the identical result, because its overflow fallback is i64::MIN == LONG_MIN.
findings.evidence:

$ /tmp/w/rs/cand -9223372036854775808 -> 0

findings.claim: The exact algorithm to implement in Rust (verified byte-identical to glibc atoi on all 322k cases) is the following, driven from args_os().nth(1) with default 18.

confirmed: Output is plain LF-terminated lines with nothing on stderr and exit code 0 -- reconfirmed directly (not through a pipe) for argv in {absent, "", "18", "abc", "-5", $'\xff', "2147483648", "9999999999999999999999", "0"}: every run gave rc=0, errbytes=0, last byte 0x0A, and zero CR bytes. Even the ERANGE-triggering overflow inputs print nothing to stderr.
stdout never lacks a trailing newline (every line is emitted with std::endl; tail -c1 is 0x0a in all cases tested, including the n<=0 short output).
`std::cout << bool` prints "1"/"0" and sizes print as plain decimal -- visible in the raw n=18 output: 18 / 1 / 1 / value_3 / modified / 18 / 18 / 14 / value_6 / 7 / 8 / 15 / 1 / 1 / default / 0 / 1.

All n <= 0 produce byte-identical output (14 lines, 40 bytes, md5 a153b11b8ec7c4b38780f930319ae45d) -- verified for n = -5,-4,-3,-2,-1,0. So a parse result of 0 is NOT distinguishable from any negative result by stdout alone.

Every n in 1..=400 produces a DISTINCT md5, so the fingerprint table is a sound oracle for recovering the parsed n from the binary's stdout in that range (I used it as the oracle for 2,361 randomized argv checks).
No-arg default n = 18: `test18_executable` with no argv[1] is byte-identical to `test18_executable 18`.

The lead engineer's parsing hypothesis (skip C isspace, one optional sign, decimal digits, accumulate saturating at i64::MAX/i64::MIN, truncate with `as i32`) HOLDS for every one of the 322,264 strings I tested -- I found no counterexample.

The reference binary is sub-linear per op and fast: n=1000000 prints its first line essentially instantly, which is what let me use timeouts to prove that n=INT_MAX inputs really are huge workloads rather than parse-to-zero.
risks: FATAL: using `std::env::args()` instead of `args_os()`. Rust's `args()` panics on non-UTF-8 argv -- `/tmp/w/rs/panicky $'\xff'` aborted with "called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: \"\\xFF\"" and exit code 101, while the C++ binary prints the n<=0 output with exit 0. Must use `std::env::args_os().nth(1)` + `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt::as_bytes()` and parse raw bytes.

Using `s.trim().parse::<i32>()` or `i32::from_str`: it rejects an empty string, a leading '+' is accepted but trailing junk ("7abc", "12.9", "1e3", "5 ") is an Err, and out-of-range is an Err rather than a wrap. All of "", "abc", "7abc", "12.9", "1e3", "0x10", "+-3" must silently become 0 / 7 / 12 / 1 / 0 / 0 respectively.

Saturating at i32 instead of truncating. If a port clamps to i32::MAX, "4294967314" would run a 2-billion-element workload instead of printing the n=18 output. The `as i32` truncation is load-bearing and is directly observable.

Saturating at the wrong width. Accumulating in u64/u128/i128 and then truncating gives 18 for "18446744073709551634", but the correct answer is -1: saturation happens at the i64 (C `long`) boundary FIRST, then truncation. Equally, saturating at i32 before ever reaching 2^63 breaks "4294967314".

Clamping negatives to 0 early (e.g. `if n < 0 { n = 0 }` during parse rather than letting the i64 value wrap through `as i32`). "-4294967278" must produce n = +18, and "-2147483649" must produce n = +2147483647. Both are negative-looking strings that yield large positive n.

Using Rust's `char::is_whitespace()` / `str::trim()` for the leading skip. Those accept U+0085, U+00A0 and the Unicode space separators; C isspace in the C locale accepts only {0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20}. I verified byte-exhaustively that no other byte is skipped, and that UTF-8 NBSP (0xC2 0xA0) before '7' yields 0, not 7.

Treating an empty argv[1] as "no argument". `argc > 1` is true for the empty string, so `test18_executable ""` must give n=0 (the n<=0 output), NOT the default 18. A port using `args_os().nth(1).filter(|s| !s.is_empty())` would be wrong.
Joining or otherwise consuming argv[2..]. Only argv[1] matters; `test18_executable 4 99` is byte-identical to `test18_executable 4`.

Rejecting or mis-handling long digit runs. A 100,000-digit string of 9s must parse to -1 (LONG_MAX truncated) with no panic and no stderr; a parser that indexes a fixed buffer or that panics on overflow in debug builds (`acc * 10 + d` without checked arithmetic -- debug Rust panics on overflow) would break. Use checked arithmetic with a latched overflow flag, and keep consuming the remaining digits.

Assuming the n<=0 collapse makes the parse result unimportant. It is safe only for results that are actually <= 0; a wrong sign or a wrong magnitude in the wrap cases ("4294967314", "-4294967278", "-2147483649") is fully observable in stdout or in runtime.

Relying on locale-aware parsing. The C++ program never calls setlocale, so LC_ALL/LANG must have zero effect; a Rust port has no locale layer, so this is only a risk if someone adds one, but note "1.5" must be 1 under de_DE too.
Emitting CRLF or omitting the final newline. Output must be exactly 14 LF-terminated lines for n<=1 (40 bytes at n<=0), 17 for n=18, with zero CR bytes and a final 0x0A.
